_comment: Odile, Chapters Two to Four: the damp season, Tam, the down-river medicine, Sallow's salt, and page forty.

lines.text: Twelve. I've opened a page for them. It's blank. I like a blank page. It means nobody owes anybody anything yet.
A working lift. Do you know what that is? It's a trade route that goes down. Nobody's ever had one of those. I've started a new ledger. It's very thin and very exciting.
Four coughs on the Commons this morning. I counted. I always count. Counting is what you do instead of screaming.
The crate went where it was needed. Don't tell me about it. I'll only put it in a column and then I'll have to look at the column.
Valve sealed, trade sealed, ledger sealed. Neat. I hate neat. Neat is what a town looks like when it's stopped.
Sallow has salt and no beets. We have beets and no salt. This is the closest thing to romance the Exchange has ever seen.
New column in the ledger: 'Coughs'. I'd like it to be the shortest column in the book. I'd like a lot of things.

tam.say: You'll have heard the coughing. The lake breathes out in the damp season and the little ones breathe it in.
I had a brother. Tam. Two years younger, all elbows. The damp came the winter I was fourteen and the medicine came from down-river eleven days after we buried him.
Eleven days. I counted them. That was when I started counting.
So, yes. I'm hard about the trade. I'm hard about the burner and the beets and the price of glowglass. Because the arithmetic of a damp winter is a small box in the ground.

choice.text: Then let's get the trade moving.

tam.say: So am I. Every year. It doesn't help, and I'd be offended if you stopped. Now buy something.
Good. Twenty glowbeets through the Exchange and the first crate goes down-river. Medicine comes back up the chute before the worst of it. If we're quick.

medicine.say: It came. Up the chute this morning, in a crate stamped with a settlement I've never seen. Bark powder. Honey. A dosing card in a careful hand.
Enough for the children on the Commons. And one crate over, because whoever packed it can't count, God love them.
If you find anyone coughing down that lift of yours, come and tell me. I'll find the arithmetic.
You've got a face. Somebody's coughing down there. Tell me who.

choice.text: Wren Askew. Barnaby's partner. She's dying of it.

medicine.say: Barnaby's Wren. Of course it is. Take it. Take it before I do the sums.
One crate. Twice a day with honey. And if she's anything like him, sit on her until she takes it.
...You're an idiot. A principled one. I'll keep it on the shelf. Shelves are patient. People less so.

medicine2.say: You came back. With a face. Somebody down there is coughing, and you've decided it's my business.
Of course it's my business. Everything is. Take the crate. Twice a day, with honey.
Don't thank me. I've put it under 'Losses'. It's the only column I'm proud of.

salt_trade.say: Salt. You brought me salt from the bottom of the world.
Salt keeps food. Food keeps people. People keep paying their debts. Do you see? It's arithmetic, all the way down.
I'll buy every grain you bring. Tell this Pell that Wick wants salt, and that Wick has beets, and that I am, generally speaking, fair.

page40.say: You know about page forty. Everyone who matters knows about page forty. It's still the best-kept secret in Wick.
If the Heart breathes and the Trunks open, this town gets bigger. Bigger towns need ledgers that aren't held together by one woman's spite.
She tears page forty out of the ledger, carefully, along the stitching, folds it twice and puts it in the stove.
Nobody owes anybody anything. Don't tell them. They'll only start behaving.
